posts.hook: Non negotiable as a {mum} who wants her {kids} outside
slides: Old clothes, bare hands, no rush. Mud is part of the lesson, not a mess to prevent.
Worms and woodlice are the main characters of any garden. Get down low and say hello.
Five minutes with the watering can after tea. Small, slow and the one bit of the day with no screen.
Even if it is one wonky carrot. Especially if it is one wonky carrot.
Child sized trowel, their own seeds, their own patch. It is theirs, so they look after it.
posts.title: Non negotiable for us: the garden belongs to the children too
posts.caption: I used to keep the garden tidy and the children out of it. Now it is the other way round, and I would not go back. Muddy knees, slow Sundays, and a small person very proud of a very small carrot 💚

posts.hook: 6 things I plan on doing with my kids every spring
slides: Plant something on the first warm day.
Anything. A pot of cress counts. The point is starting the season together.
Jam jar, magnifying glass, and one rule: everyone goes home again.
Each child picks a vegetable and keeps a little patch. Arguments about whose is growing faster are part of the tradition.
Blanket on the grass, one chapter, no phones. The book travels with us.
Radishes come up fast, so the wait is short and the pride is big.
A drawing a week. By summer it is the best photo album we own.
posts.title: Our spring list, written down so we actually do it
posts.caption: Nothing fancy and nothing that needs a trip anywhere. Just a little list on the fridge that gets us outside together every spring. What would you add to yours?

hook_box: I could not find a garden kit my kids would actually finish
posts.title: So I made one: a garden kit and a book in one box
posts.caption: Every kit I tried was either all pieces and no story, or all story and nothing to dig. So I put the two together: seeds, tools and a picture book for little hands. Link in bio if you want to see inside 🌱

posts.hook: What they actually need to start gardening with kids
slides: A pot, some soil, a few seeds and a small spade. That is the whole list.
Even a window box. Ownership is what keeps a small person coming back.
You do not need to know the names of anything. Just look closely together and ask what is that?
A story to hang it on.
A book turns a pot of soil into an adventure, and bedtime gets a reason to talk about tomorrow's watering.
Seeds take their time. So does everything worth having.
posts.title: You do not need a big garden, just a small start
posts.caption: When people ask where to begin, I tell them to begin smaller than feels worth it. One pot, one packet, one child with a spoon. The rest follows 🌱

posts.hook: 6 cosy things to grow on a windowsill this winter
slides: Ready in a week, and it counts as a first harvest.
Snip a few leaves for a sandwich. The best lunch of the month.
Any old mug with a hole in the bottom, a saucer underneath and a label in wobbly handwriting.
Beans between wet paper and the glass. You can watch the roots appear.
Pick the page you liked best and grow that. Then read it again while you wait.
posts.title: Grey outside, green on the windowsill
posts.caption: Winter afternoons are long, and a windowsill of small green things makes them shorter. Which one would you start with?

posts.hook: POV: your three year old pulls up their first ever carrot
slides: Both hands, full effort, a very serious face.
Part disbelief, part triumph. It is a carrot the size of a finger and it is the best thing they have ever done.
Wash it, snap it, eat it on the spot. No notes.
posts.title: The most proud face I have ever seen on a three year old
posts.caption: Small carrot, enormous pride. This is why we grow things with the children 🥕
